# Conclusions

Overall, this project suggests that data centers are not simply built in isolated rural areas, but are instead closely associated with more urban and populous counties. Our clustering results showed a clear difference between counties with very few data centers and counties with many, even when the clustering model had no direct access to data center counts. At the same time, our difference-in-difference results point to a mixed local economic impact: data centers appear to be associated with lower personal income and declines in some sectors of employment, but also with lower unemployment, increased construction activity, and lower $\text{PM}_{2.5}$ air pollution in certain cases. Together, these findings suggest that data centers bring real local trade-offs rather than uniform economic benefits or downsides. While our use of NAICS 518 is not a perfect measure of true data centers, it provided a consistent and replicable way to study this issue using public data. More broadly, this project demonstrates that data center locations and their impacts are tied to local county characteristics in ways that deserve further attention as global dependence on data center infrastructure continues to grow.
